newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH SOCIAL SPENDING CUTS MAY NOT BE OVER - GOVT.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH SOCIAL SPENDING CUTS MAY NOT BE OVER - GOVT.

text.p: Finnish social security spending may be cut further if balancing the state finances requires new savings, the government said on Tuesday.
"If the balancing of the state finances requires additional savings, social security may again face the need of savings," the government said in a report to parliament.
The final version of the report deleted a statement in a late draft that most decisions regarding social security spending cuts and structural reforms had already been made.
The deletion was made at Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's request, an official at the ministry of social and health affairs (STM) told Reuters.

Lipponen's reasoning had been that although most decisions on social security outright spending cuts had been made, decisions on structural reforms of systems were still being prepared, the official said.
Elsewhere in the report, the government said income gaps between various groups in society may grow if transfers to households had to be cut again.
The drive to meet convergence criteria for the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) might force Finland and other EU countries to cut social security spending, it said.
"Times of austere fiscal and monetary policy lie ahead for EU countries. This may bring additional pressures on the financing of social security," the Finnish government said.

For the EU in general and Finland in particular, high unemployment is putting the heaviest burden on social security. The unemployment trend would be crucial for social security spending in the next few years, it said.
Lower unemployment would reduce the cost of jobless benefits and other social security allowances, and boost tax and social security contribution revenue, the report noted.
But the outlook for Finnish unemployment was bleak, it said.
"High unemployment, especially long-term unemployment, threatens to become a permanent phenomenon in the Finnish society," it said.
This echoed an October 2 government report, which said high unemployment was likely to remain a problem for about 15 years.

The new report also repeated that in the long term, the ageing of the population -- Finland has the fastest-growing share of the aged in its population in the EU -- would pose a big challenge for the social security system.
In 10 to 15 years it said the age structure would become significantly less advantageous in terms of financing pensions. In the year 2020, one third of all Finns would be over 60 years old, it added.
No direct comparison was available, but according to Statistics Finland, 14 percent of Finns were 65 years or older in 1994, while 24 percent were 45-64 years old.
In the report, Lipponen's coalition government said its aim was to retain a good level of social security coverage, and that the level of benefits would be moderate.
"In developing unemployment security, choices must be made between the level of benefits, the duration of pay-outs and the requirements to qualify as a recipient," the report said.

The responsibility for financing social security through contributions by the state, private sector employers and the insured themselves should be clearly defined, and the financing principles should be sustainable, it said.
Social security financing should be developed in a way that strengthened the system's ability to tolerate cyclical changes, the report said.
It did not elaborate, but said work was underway to reform employers' contributions to promote employment.
"In what way capital income and assets should affect social security is also being studied," the report said, but gave no details.

In a European perspective, it was important to keep social policy decision-making in national hands, while ensuring that no EU-country used clearly lower social security costs as a tool to boost competitiveness, it said.

In Finland, social security expenditure to GDP, which peaked at 38 percent in 1993 and would fall to 34 percent this year, could fall further towards the EU-average (27.8 percent in 1993) by the end of this decade, the government said.
This will hinge on favourable economic growth and employment trends, it added.
